angleRead.name: Elliot Marbury
angleRead.text: Vinnie Keane's 2041 line is the newest entry in a 17-season dossier, and it reads like two different hitters depending on which column you look at. The slugging is absurd — one homer every 9.8 at-bats — but the walk column is empty and the strikeout rate, one every 21.2 at-bats, is the tightest of the entire run. That is the hinge: a 37-game slice where the power is real but the plate discipline looks like a ghost of the 2039 season, when he was whiffing once every 2.0 at-bats. The question is which number is the outlier. You could be looking at a hitter who found something late, or you could be looking at a small-sample illusion that flatters a fading skill. The peer band makes it weirder,

plan.focus: The 2041 strikeout rate (one every 21.2 at-bats) versus the 2039 rate (one every 2.0 at-bats) as the defining tension in Keane's late-career profile.
plan.why: Because a 127-at-bat sample is too small to call a transformation, but the gap between the 2041 and 2039 strikeout rates is too large to ignore. The 2038 season — 49 homers, one every 6.7 at-bats — is the only full-season baseline that makes the 2041 power look normal, and it is three years old. The line needs to be read against the full 2036-2041 window to see which seasons are the true signal and which are noise.

unverifiedLead: The 2041 strikeout rate may be a fluke of a short season, but it is worth asking whether Keane changed his swing or approach in the offseason.
The 2039 season's high strikeout rate may have been an injury-related anomaly, not a skill baseline.
